idiom_name: sync.OnceValue accessor (or sync.Once.Do inside the stand-in)
implementation_notes: Go usually collapses the stand-in into an accessor: sync.OnceValue(func() *Image { return loadImage(path) }) (Go 1.21) returns a function that builds the value on the first call and returns the same value forever, with sync.OnceValues for a value plus error; sync.Once.Do is the older form for an initializer with no result. Because interfaces are implicit, any struct that satisfies the interface can act as the stand-in, so the classic class structure is rarely written out, and the stdlib primitive carries the exactly-once guarantee and the happens-before edge. Hand-write the stand-in struct when the deferral must be per-instance, when the subject must be refreshable, or when several methods must share the guard, since a package-level OnceValue is process-wide.
pitfalls: Once.Do deadlocks if the initializer calls Do on the same Once, and a panic inside f is remembered: Once considers the call done, so later calls return without retrying (OnceValue re-panics with the same value).
A copied sync.Once (or a struct containing one) is broken - Once must not be copied after first use, and a package-level OnceValue is shared process-wide, not per instance.
The produced value is shared by every caller, so the real subject must be safe for concurrent use or must be protected by its own mutex.
